extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys (patent practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103, including treatment of prior art, analogous art, differences between prior art and claimed invention, and consideration of applicant rebuttal evidence. Intended to direct examiners and inform practitioners on evidentiary and analytical requirements during examination and prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant burden to rebut obviousness findings; 37 CFR 1.111(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Office finds that the claimed invention would have been obvious, the burden shifts to the applicant to (A) show that the Office erred in these findings or (B) provide other evidence to show that the claimed subject matter would have been nonobvious. 37 CFR 1.111(b) requires applicant to distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references. If an applicant disagrees with any factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred substantively as to the factual findings. A mere statement or argument that the Office has not established a prima facie case of obviousness or that the Office’s reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence will not be considered substantively adequate. Office personnel may repeat the prior rejection and make the next Office action final (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence and secondary considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all rebuttal evidence that is timely presented by the applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include 'secondary considerations' such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, and evidence of unexpected results (Graham v. John Deere). Once rebuttal evidence is presented, Office personnel should reconsider the initial obviousness determination in view of the entire record (see In re Piasecki; In re Eli Lilly & Co.). All rejections and proposed rejections should be reviewed to confirm continued viability. The Office action should clearly communicate findings and conclusions and articulate how conclusions are supported by the findings. Follow procedures in MPEP §706.07(a). See MPEP §2145 and §716–§716.10 for affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 for traversing grounds of rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 can be used under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. §102 can be used to support a rejection under section 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art can be relied upon for anticipation and obviousness determinations regardless of statutory category. A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection is based on the applicable 35 U.S.C. 102 provision (e.g., 102(a)(1)/(a)(2) or pre-AIA 102(a), 102(b), 102(e), etc.) depending on the reference type and dates. Examples: an issued U.S. patent older than one year can operate as a statutory bar under pre-AIA 102(b); publications that could be sworne-behind may be overcome with affidavits under 37 CFR 1.131. See MPEP §§901–901.06(d), §2121–§2129, and §2151–§2155 for overview and details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of the prior art must be evaluated (enablement, inoperative devices, admissions, breadth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must assess the substantive content of prior art with respect to issues such as availability of inoperative devices, whether prior art must be enabling, and whether a reference provides a broad disclosure versus only preferred embodiments or admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2121–§2129 for case law and discussion on how these factors affect whether a reference can support anticipation or obviousness (examples: when a prior art device is inoperative, whether broad disclosures are sufficient, treatment of admissions). The evaluation concerns not just the existence of references but their substantive teaching and applicability to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine content of prior art as of the time the invention was made to avoid hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art must be determined at the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight in obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The decisionmaker must 'cast the mind back to the time the invention was made' and consider what a person of ordinary skill would have known then (W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock). See MPEP §2145 subsection X.A. for discussion on rebutting applicants’ hindsight arguments. Examiners should avoid using knowledge of the invention to reinterpret prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) — evidence required to show conditions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to avail themselves of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(c) benefits bears the burden of establishing that subject matter used in a rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish joint research agreement benefits (for applications pending on or after December 10, 2004), applicant must show: (A) claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on or before the invention date; (B) the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the joint research agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the names of the parties to the joint research agreement. This disqualification applies only to subject matter qualifying as prior art under subsections (e), (f), or (g) of pre‑AIA 35 U.S.C. 102. See MPEP §2146.01 and §2146.02 and In re Bartfeld for limits and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous prior art requirement for 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. 103, the reference must be analogous art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous art if: (1) the reference is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if it addresses a different problem); or (2) the reference is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor (even if not in the same field). Reasonably pertinent means it would 'logically have commended itself to an inventor's attention' in considering the problem. Examiners must determine analogous art and may include a statement of their understanding of the problem. Applicant arguments that the examiner misconstrued the problem (and thus improperly relied on nonanalogous art) should be fully considered and evaluated against the specification and inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw. See In re Bigio, In re ICON, In re Klein, In re Clay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners should consider similarities and differences in structure and function (over classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: When assessing whether art is analogous, similarities and differences in structure and function carry greater weight than Patent Office classification or class cross-references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent classification and cross-references are some evidence of (non)analogy, but courts have emphasized structural and functional comparisons as more important (see In re Ellis). Examiners should analyze how the inventions operate and are structured, not rely solely on class headings or search notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy guidance in the chemical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the chemical arts, references are analogous when their teachings would be pertinent to the problems addressed by the claimed invention, even if from different named arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Ex parte Bland – references concerning absorbing biologically active materials on carriers were pertinent across related problems; Stratoflex v. Aeroquip – solutions in PTFE vs rubber hose art were analogous because manufacturers and problems overlapped; In re Mlot-Fijalkowski – dye chemistry references were pertinent because the problem was one of dye chemistry. Examiners should consider the nature of the problem (e.g., chemistry) rather than narrow field labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy guidance in the mechanical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mechanical arts, a broad spectrum of prior art may be explored where one of ordinary skill would be aware that similar problems exist in different areas; structural and functional overlap supports analogy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stevenson v. ITC; In re Bigio (toothbrush vs hair brush). Cases show that when structure and function are essentially the same (e.g., double-acting pumps/compressors), references from different but related mechanical fields may be analogous. Examiners should consider whether a person skilled in the art would look to the other area to solve the same or similar problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy guidance in the electrical arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In electrical arts, references solving the same technical problem (e.g., rate-limiting) in different high-power/high-frequency contexts may be analogous to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers — circuits used in high-power, high-frequency devices that inhibited runaway pulses were analogous to pacemaker designer art facing a rate-limiting problem. Examiners should consider whether a person skilled in the relevant electrical subfield would reasonably consult the other art for solutions to the same problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy guidance in the design arts
rubrics_metrics.description: In design patent applications, analogous art determination follows specific case law; prior designs of contemporaneous furniture or related items may be analogous depending on general use and designer knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §1504.03 and examples: In re Rosen (contemporary furniture designs analogous), Ex parte Pappas (architectural handbook analogous to feed bunk design), In re Butera (metal ball anode design was nonanalogous to insect repellent/air freshener design). Examiners should assess whether prior designs are of the 'type claimed' and whether a designer of ordinary skill would have reason to look to those references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider the claimed invention as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences between prior art and the claims requires interpreting the claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question under 35 U.S.C. 103 is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious, not whether specific differences alone would have been obvious. See MPEP §2111–§2116.01 and examples (Stratoflex; Schenck v. Nortron). Examiners must avoid overemphasizing one structural difference while ignoring other claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill an invention down to a 'gist' or 'thrust' (anti‑pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distilling an invention down to the 'gist' or 'thrust' disregards the requirement of analyzing the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (W.L. Gore; Bausch & Lomb v. Barnes-Hind; Jones v. Hardy; Panduit) show that focusing on an advantage or single limitation while disregarding express claim limitations improperly treats claims as if they read differently than allowed. Examiners should analyze all claim limitations and contexts rather than abstracting the invention to a one-word or narrow gist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of source/cause of a problem is part of 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Discovery of the source of a problem can be part of the subject matter considered 'as a whole' and may support patentability even if the remedy would be obvious once the source is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Sponnoble: discovering the source of a problem may render a combination patentable; however, if prior art contains the same solution for a similar problem, the discovery may not produce patentable subject matter (see In re Wiseman). Examiners should analyze whether the discovery itself is supported and whether prior art teaches the same solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who allege the inventor discovered the source of a problem must provide evidence substantiating the allegation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be affidavits or declarations, or a clear and persuasive assertion in the specification. Unsubstantiated statements of counsel are insufficient (see In re Wiseman; In re Kaslow). Examiners should require sufficient evidentiary support when applicants assert discovery-based patentability arguments.
